definition.text: Running a business so that it makes money while keeping its harm to the environment, local communities and society as small as possible.

facts.text: Such firms aim at the triple bottom line of profit, people and planet, weighing environmental, economic and social factors in their decisions.
A green business offers products that cut demand for harmful ones, keeps its finances sound, respects human rights and supports inclusion of local and global communities.
The idea grew out of late-20th-century debates on sustainable development; the 1987 report Our Common Future shaped how private firms thought about managing the environment.
A central aim is to cut the environmental harm from making and using goods, for example by measuring carbon footprints, cutting waste and redesigning products to last longer.
The business historian Geoffrey Jones traces green business back to start-ups in organic food and wind and solar energy before World War 1.
If a firm's whole model is unsustainable, becoming sustainable can mean rebuilding it, for example moving from selling cars to offering car sharing.
Firms often meet only the lowest standards; real sustainability is said to need a purpose that goes beyond legal compliance.

title: Corporate environmental responsibility

definition.text: A company's duty to avoid damaging the natural environment.

facts.text: The term comes from corporate social responsibility (CSR); CER deals strictly with environmental effects inside company strategy, while CSR leans toward social matters.
Protecting the environment used to be seen as the government's job, done through rules and penalties; the private sector has since taken on a shared responsibility.
Its main elements are using resources efficiently and limiting activities that would spoil resources for future generations.
Its main drivers are government policies and rules, backed by subsidies, tariffs and taxes, plus pressure from media, the public, shareholders and NGOs.
Obstacles include the cost of regulation, uncertain economic gains, expensive new technology and rules that differ from country to country.
It is unclear which emissions a firm answers for when they are spread across suppliers and outsourcing, or whether it should answer for past emissions made before the harm was known.
Stakeholders' growing awareness of how much harm business does to the environment has made it more institutionalized.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether firms must go beyond the law or should first make profits for shareholders, and on which emissions a firm is responsible for.

title: Circular business models

definition.text: Ways of running a business that cut resource use and waste and regenerate natural systems by rethinking how goods are made and used.

facts.text: Early talk of circularity centred on 're-X' steps such as recycling, remanufacturing, reuse and recovery.
Four strategies: narrowing loops (using fewer materials), slowing loops (repair, reuse, resale, rental), closing loops (recycling into new production) and regenerating natural systems.
They can cut costs and create new offers, but face hurdles in technology, consumer habits and profitability.

notes: The Circular economy page also has a 'Circular business models' section; it may duplicate an entry in the circular-and-bio-based-economies chapter.

definition.text: Plans a company uses to win new revenue from sustainability while guarding against rising energy, regulation and resource costs and shifting customer views.

facts.text: Common strategies are innovation, collaboration, process improvement and sustainability reporting, plus greening the supply chain.
The Sustainability Balanced Scorecard measures performance by balancing financial and non-financial, short- and long-term goals, building environmental and social aims into management.
A 2023 Swiss survey of 514 small and medium firms found 89% had never produced a sustainability report.

definition.text: A business's responsibility for the well-being of its employees, customers and community.

facts.text: Firms contribute by supporting education, encouraging staff to volunteer and giving to charity.
It is often tied to environmental justice: social fairness and environmental care affect each other.

title: Sustainability and financial performance

definition.text: The debate over whether a company's environmental and social efforts raise or lower its profits.

facts.text: A positive link between environmental performance and economic performance has been reported.
A 2026 study of Indian firms found that steady improvement in environmental performance went with better financial results.
A 2023 study of European listed firms found the opposite of a 'win-win': stronger sustainability practices went with lower profitability, at least for a time.
Studies link sustainability practices to financial success and customer satisfaction, but mostly at larger firms with more money to spend on them.
Gains can include attracting staff, tax breaks and new markets.

contested_note: Some studies find sustainability raises financial performance while a 2023 study of European firms found it lowered profitability.
notes: Passes test 5: discussed on Sustainable business, Corporate environmental responsibility and Corporate social responsibility (see part02).

title: Strategic support for environmental regulation
article: Corporate environmental responsibility#Benefits of corporate environmental responsibility

definition.text: A firm backing new environmental rules because they will hurt its competitors more than itself.

facts.text: Many firms find it pays to argue for environmental rules and prepare for them before they become law.
One study found firms support climate laws to gain power over competitors, accepting short-term costs to come out ahead in the long run.

definition.text: A design approach that cuts a product's or service's harm to health and the environment, counting impacts across its whole life cycle.

facts.text: Its four parts are cleaner processing and manufacturing, greener packaging, design for disposal or reuse, and energy efficiency.
Life-cycle assessment is used to compare design options and pick the least harmful.
Claimed benefits are cost savings, lower risk, new market openings and meeting regulations.
Sustainable business leaders treat it as part of their work, along with counting life-cycle costs.
